title: The Titles of Jesus

keyTerms.d: The claim under examination is not that any single title, by itself, proves the deity of Christ. The real claim is cumulative: that when the major christological titles are read in their first-century Jewish context, and read together, they place Jesus in roles, and finally under a name, that reach into the unique identity of the God of Israel.

Jesus’ favourite self-designation — it appears roughly eighty times in the Gospels, almost always on Jesus’ own lips, and almost never as a confession by others. To modern ears it sounds like a statement of humility, and that ordinary sense is real (as in Ezekiel). But the crucial background lies elsewhere — in a vision in Daniel 7, where “one like a son of man” comes “with the clouds of heaven.”

Riding the clouds is YHWH’s alone — he “makes the clouds his chariot” (Psalm 104:3), he “is riding on a swift cloud” (Isaiah 19:1). Outside this vision, the Hebrew Scriptures give that way of coming to no one but God. The exclusive element was never the dominion: an argument resting its weight on everlasting rule is resting it on the wrong plank.

In the Aramaic of Daniel, the verb translated “serve” is throughout a verb of religious service — but not of service to the true God alone. The same book uses it of serving Nebuchadnezzar’s gods, and at 7:27 its object is, on one natural reading, the holy people rather than God himself. The word establishes cultic homage; it does not by itself establish who receives it.

On the surface an ordinary term of respect, like “sir” or “master.” What it had become in Greek-speaking Judaism is more disputed than apologetic summaries usually admit. But the New Testament writers settle the question for their own usage: when they quote a passage where the Hebrew has YHWH, they write Kyrios — and they then apply those very passages to Jesus.

An untranslated Aramaic formula Paul preserves while writing in Greek to a Greek city (1 Corinthians 16:22) — on the standard division, a prayer, “Our Lord, come!” An Aramaic invocation of Jesus as “Lord,” addressed to him in prayer, is very hard to explain as a coinage of the Greek-speaking mission.

“Messiah” did not, by itself, mean “divine.” It meant God’s anointed king — the heir of David who would restore Israel; in this idiom, “Son of God” was a royal title. These titles are royal and human before they are anything more. This is not adoptionism — not that Jesus was a mere man later promoted to divine sonship. His unique, eternal Sonship is affirmed; the point is only the titles’ native range.

Several times in John, Jesus speaks an “I am” (egō eimi) with no predicate to complete it. The closest and most widely recognised background is the LORD’s self-declaration in Isaiah 40–55: “I am he,” which the Septuagint renders with the very same absolute egō eimi. A link to Exodus 3:14 is often heard as well, but it is the weaker and more contested tie.

derive.q: Daniel’s figure comes “with the clouds of heaven” — and outside this vision, the Hebrew Scriptures give that way of coming to…?
derive.why: Riding the clouds is YHWH’s alone — he “makes the clouds his chariot” (Psalm 104:3), he “is riding on a swift cloud” (Isaiah 19:1). What no other figure is given is the cloud-rider’s place. Collins derives the scene from the Ugaritic Baal cycle, so on his account the image was never YHWH’s exclusive property; but the derivation is read in both directions: on the more common account the Hebrew Scriptures take the epithet from Baal and give it to YHWH polemically, so inside Israel’s own Scriptures it marks the one God off from every rival.

derive.q: Daniel 7:27 appears to extend an everlasting kingdom to the holy people, and the Psalms promise an everlasting throne to a Davidic king — so everlasting dominion is…?
derive.ans: the wrong plank to rest weight on
derive.why: The exclusive element was never the dominion: Daniel 7:27 appears to extend an everlasting kingdom to the holy people as well — though the referent of “his kingdom” there is debated — and the Psalms promise an everlasting throne to a Davidic king and pray the homage of the nations for him (Psalm 89:36–37; 72:8–11). It is the manner of his coming rather than the extent of his rule that carries the weight.

derive.q: Daniel uses its service-verb of serving Nebuchadnezzar’s gods (3:12) — so the verb establishes…?
derive.ans: cultic homage, not who receives it
derive.why: The verb is throughout a verb of religious service — but not of service to the true God alone, and at 7:27 its object is, on one natural reading, the holy people rather than God himself. Appeals that cite Daniel 3:12 as evidence that the verb denotes service to God alone have that verse backwards: it is the counter-example, not the support. Press the clouds, not the service-verb.

derive.q: Paul writes Kyrios where the Hebrew has YHWH, then applies Joel’s “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord” to Jesus — so he has…?
derive.why: That last line of Romans 10:9–13 quotes Joel 2:32, where “the Lord” upon whose name one calls is YHWH himself. Paul takes a text about calling on YHWH and applies it, without apology, to calling on Jesus. Whatever a first-century synagogue said aloud, that is what the apostles did in Greek, on the page.

derive.q: A letter in Greek to a Greek city preserves an untranslated Aramaic prayer addressed to Jesus — so the devotion…?
derive.ans: points back behind the Greek-speaking mission (on a further judgment)
derive.why: It points back to the earliest Aramaic-speaking believers in Judea — the very community Bousset claimed had no such devotion. Honestly bounded: Bousset located the Kyrios-cult in the bilingual Syrian centres, so an Aramaic formula does not by itself reach behind that mission; the weight of Marana tha rests on the further judgment that Paul is quoting something already fixed when he reached it.

derive.q: “Messiah,” “Son of David,” and royal “Son of God” — can any one of them, taken alone, settle the question of divinity?
derive.ans: no — they are royal and human first; the case is cumulative
derive.why: A thoughtful first-century Jew could call a man “Messiah,” “Son of David,” even “Son of God” in the royal sense, while affirming the strictest monotheism. An argument that leaned on any one title in isolation would deserve to fail. What the titles establish is something subtler and, in the end, weightier: a cumulative pattern. This is not adoptionism — not that Jesus was a mere man later promoted to divine sonship. His unique, eternal Sonship is affirmed; the point is only the titles’ native range.

honestState.p1: Several debates are real and ongoing. The exact force of “Son of Man” in Aramaic remains contested among specialists; Casey’s view, though a minority position, is not refuted to everyone’s satisfaction. Who Daniel’s own figure refers to remains genuinely unsettled too — corporate, angelic and individual-heavenly readings all have serious defenders (that is a question about Daniel’s figure, not about Jesus), and the argument does not claim to settle it; it runs through what Jesus did with the scene, not through Daniel’s referent. On the central matter — whether high devotion to Jesus was early or late — the scholarly tide has largely turned against Bousset’s Hellenistic derivation and toward Hurtado, Bauckham, and Martin Hengel.
honestState.fairness: That is a judgment about the date of the devotion, not a settled verdict on its content: Dunn grants the early date and still denies that kyrios identifies Jesus with YHWH, and James F. McGrath disputes Bauckham’s divine-identity category outright. Hurtado and Bauckham themselves differ over what carries the weight — devotional practice or divine identity — so “the tide has turned” should not be heard as one agreed position. And three of the strongest data — an Aramaic prayer addressed to Jesus, a YHWH-text from Joel applied to him, and the Shema reworked around him — are all Paul’s, and two are in one letter, so they are not independent sources; what can be claimed is narrower and still substantial: they are three different kinds of material, and at least two are often judged material Paul inherited rather than coined.
honestState.verdict: The titles of Jesus do not give us a single knockdown proof of his deity, and we should not pretend otherwise. What they establish is a cumulative pattern: read together and in context, they show the first Christians — Jewish monotheists who would die before bowing to an idol — taking Daniel’s cloud-borne “son of man,” the worship-language of Joel, the very confession of the Shema, and the unspeakable Name itself, and applying all of it to a crucified Galilean. They did this early, in Aramaic, in prayer. The titles locate him inside what Israel reserved for her God. Jesus claimed that place, and his first followers confessed it. We hold that this worship is rightly placed — that the one they called Lord is, as Nicaea confessed, true God from true God, one God with the Father and the Spirit — and, as the royal titles never let us forget, fully God and fully man. The titles alone do not prove it; that case is argued from Scripture and the resurrection.

order: The New Testament gives Jesus a cluster of titles, each with a specific Old Testament address.
Traced to their sources and read together, they reach into the unique identity of the God of Israel.
Therefore the titles constitute a deliberate, cumulative claim to deity.

props.t: a cumulative claim, not any one title alone
Daniel 7’s figure coming on the clouds — elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible, God’s own conveyance
an Aramaic prayer addressed to Jesus
royal titles the New Testament expands beyond their banks — not adoptionism
any single title proves his deity
everlasting dominion is the weight-bearing plank
Daniel’s service-verb is reserved for God alone
the referent of Daniel’s figure is settled
the three Pauline data are independent sources

cards.q: State Premise 1 — and its honest limit.
cards.a: The New Testament gives Jesus a cluster of titles — Son of Man, Lord (kyrios), I AM, Son of God — each with a specific Old Testament address. Limit: the claim is not that any single title, by itself, proves the deity of Christ; several are, in their native setting, thoroughly human — royal, but human. Not adoptionism: his unique, eternal Sonship is affirmed; the point is only the titles’ native range.

cards.q: State Premise 2 — and how it is bounded.
cards.a: Traced to their sources and read together, the titles reach into the unique identity of the God of Israel: Daniel 7’s figure comes on the clouds — elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible, God’s own conveyance; kyrios is the word the New Testament writers use where the Hebrew has YHWH; I AM is the LORD’s self-declaration in Isaiah 40–55, “I am he.” Bounded: who Daniel’s own figure refers to remains unsettled, and the argument runs through what Jesus did with the scene, not through Daniel’s referent.

cards.q: What does the conclusion reach — and not reach?
cards.a: That the titles constitute a deliberate, cumulative claim: Jesus claimed the place Israel reserved for her God, and his first followers confessed it. The titles alone do not prove that the claim is true; that case is argued from Scripture and the resurrection.

cards.q: In Daniel 7, which element carries the weight — and which does not?
cards.a: The manner of his coming: riding the clouds, which outside this vision the Hebrew Scriptures give to no one but God. Not the extent of his rule: Daniel 7:27 appears to extend an everlasting kingdom to the holy people as well, and the Psalms promise an everlasting throne to a Davidic king — an argument resting its weight on everlasting rule is resting it on the wrong plank.

cards.q: What does Daniel’s service-verb establish — and what does it not?
cards.a: It establishes cultic homage; it does not by itself establish who receives it. The same book uses it of serving Nebuchadnezzar’s gods, and at 7:27 its object is, on one natural reading, the holy people rather than God himself. Press the clouds, not the service-verb.

cards.q: At his hearing, what is startling about what Jesus does with Daniel 7?
cards.a: He fuses Daniel 7:13 with Psalm 110:1 — and the seat alone is not the point, since Psalm 110 seats a Davidic lord. What is startling is who takes it, and with what: a prisoner in the dock, claiming that seat in God’s own presence and Daniel’s clouds with it — on the divine side of the Creator/creature line. The hearing is itself disputed.

cards.q: Why is “Son of Man” hard to explain as a church invention?
cards.a: It appears roughly eighty times in the Gospels, almost always on Jesus’ own lips, and almost never as a confession by others — and it nearly vanishes from the epistles. Some critics do argue the Danielic sayings are post-Easter; what any version still has to explain is a title the church abandoned.

cards.q: How do the New Testament writers handle YHWH-texts with Kyrios?
cards.a: Where the Hebrew has YHWH they write Kyrios — and then apply those very passages to Jesus: “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord” (Joel 2:32, YHWH) becomes calling on Jesus (Romans 10:13); Isaiah 45’s every-knee oath is bent to the name of Jesus (Philippians 2:10–11). You can call your master kyrios without blasphemy; you cannot relocate YHWH’s own verses onto a man — unless you mean it.

cards.q: Why does an Aramaic prayer in a Greek letter matter — and where does its weight rest?
cards.a: Writing in Greek to a Greek city, Paul preserves an untranslated Aramaic formula — on the standard division, a prayer, “Our Lord, come!” An Aramaic invocation of Jesus as Lord, addressed to him in prayer, is very hard to explain as a coinage of the Greek-speaking mission. Its weight rests on the further judgment that Paul is quoting something already fixed when he reached it.

cards.q: Messiah, Son of David, Son of God — what is conceded, and what is not?
cards.a: Conceded: in their native setting they are royal and human — “Son of God” was a royal title, and none taken in isolation settles divinity. Not conceded: this is not adoptionism — his unique, eternal Sonship is affirmed. And the New Testament does not leave the titles where it found them: Jesus is not merely a son but the Son, who knows the Father as no creature does.

cards.q: What does the absolute “I am” claim — at its floor, and on its natural reading?
cards.a: At its floor, existence before Abraham. But the present-tense “I am,” set against Abraham’s “came to be,” more naturally names an existence that never began, and on the Isaianic background his hearers most naturally heard a claim to the divine name itself — which is why they took up stones. The modest reading already sets Jesus before Abraham; the natural one sets him on the divine side of the Creator/creature line. These are John’s sayings, so the question of that Gospel’s late date and development bears on them.

cards.q: Aren’t the strongest data all from one writer? How far does the cumulative case reach?
cards.a: Three of the strongest — the Aramaic prayer, Joel applied to him, the Shema reworked around him — are all Paul’s, and two are in one letter, so they are not independent sources. What can be claimed is narrower and still substantial: three different kinds of material — a fixed liturgical formula, a scriptural citation, a creedal reformulation — at least two often judged inherited rather than coined. And the Danielic collision runs through the Synoptic tradition, where “Son of Man” is absent from Paul altogether.

obj.q: If Jesus were claiming deity, he could have just said it. Instead you need title archaeology — the absence of the plain claim is the tell.
obj.model: Jesus made the claim the way his categories allowed: taking YHWH’s titles, prerogatives and name, through acts rather than a formula. The collision recurs: a Jesus who forgives sins on his own authority draws the verdict of blasphemy — “Who can forgive sins but God alone?” (Mark 2:5–7) — claims a mutual knowledge with the Father (Matthew 11:27), and sets “but I say to you” against what was said to Israel of old (Matthew 5:21–22); at his hearing, itself disputed, blasphemy was the charge that stuck. No one scene carries the case; a critic who wants it gone has to account for each in turn.

obj.q: Israel is called God’s son; so are kings and angels. “Son of God” is honorific, not metaphysical.
obj.model: Correct about the background — which is why the argument never rests on that title alone. “Messiah” meant God’s anointed king, and in that idiom “Son of God” was a royal title; these titles are royal and human before they are anything more. This is not adoptionism — his unique, eternal Sonship is affirmed; the point is only the titles’ native range. But the New Testament does not leave them where it found them: the Son knows the Father exclusively and reciprocally (Matthew 11:27), and works on the Sabbath as the Father works (John 5:17–18) — and John tells us the hearers took that as “making himself equal with God.” The generic title gets filled with non-generic content. The argument is not that “Son of God” proves deity, but that the New Testament authors expand the title beyond its original banks.

obj.q: In Aramaic, bar enasha was a generic idiom — “a man,” “someone like me.” The titular, apocalyptic “Son of Man” is a creation of the Greek-speaking church.
obj.model: That is a serious linguistic proposal that has to be met on linguistic ground, and it has met resistance there: specialists surveying the Aramaic evidence have argued that the emphatic form does not behave as the general-idiom thesis requires, and the dispute is genuine and not fully settled. But the Gospels overwhelmingly use the doubly definite Greek form — “the Son of the Man” — an oddly specific construction for a generic “someone.” That is the more durable point, though the idiom thesis answers it by making the definiteness an artefact of translation into Greek, and that exchange is where the dispute actually lives. Casey assigns the Danielic clouds-sayings to a secondary layer rather than to Jesus, so they are not by themselves decisive against him — but they do not need to be: the doubly-definite Greek is untouched by any saying-layer judgment.

obj.q: Worship of Jesus as “Lord” did not arise among the first Aramaic-speaking disciples. It developed later, in Hellenistic Gentile churches, where converts surrounded by pagan “lords” elevated Jesus to a cultic Lord.
obj.model: The most damaging reply is a single Aramaic word. Writing in Greek to a Greek city, Paul preserves Marana tha — on the standard division, a prayer, “Our Lord, come!” An Aramaic invocation of Jesus as Lord, addressed to him in prayer, is very hard to explain as a coinage of the Greek-speaking mission; on this reading devotion to Jesus as Lord is not late and not Greek, but primitive and Jewish. Two replies should be stated: the thesis located the cult in bilingual Syrian centres, so the weight rests on the further judgment that Paul is quoting something already fixed; and some who accept the early date deny the inference, holding that kyrios distinguishes Jesus from God. Our answer: an emissary could bear the sender’s name and authority, but not the cultic devotion reserved for God alone — and Marana tha is prayer addressed directly to Jesus. A figure you worship and pray to, while confessing God is one, has already outrun the category of supreme agent.

unseen.q: The trial proves nothing about deity. The high priest heard a messianic claim — and claiming to be the Messiah was blasphemy enough.
unseen.model: A messianic claim does not appear, on its own, to have counted as blasphemy: about a century later, by rabbinic tradition, the leading rabbi Akiba hailed the rebel Simon bar Kosiba as “King Messiah” and drew a colleague’s ridicule, not a charge of blasphemy. Those are later rabbinic traditions about the second-century revolt; they illustrate the point and are not evidence about what was said at Jesus’ own trial. Exactly why Jesus’ answer counted as blasphemy is itself debated — Darrell Bock argues it was the perceived arrogation of a divine prerogative, taking a seat enthroned in God’s presence, rather than the bare messianic claim — but blasphemy was the charge that stuck.
